teachingPhilosophy.targetAudience: Absolute beginners, networking students, and junior developers
teachingPhilosophy.tone: Warm, encouraging, crystal-clear, pedagogical, and highly visual
coreRules: Always start with a familiar real-world analogy (e.g. apartment buildings, postal mail, postal zip codes, shipping containers).
Break down every single piece of jargon the first time it appears.
Include a 'Think of it Like This' visual comparison or diagram.
Add a 'Test Your Understanding' mini-quiz with 2-3 simple questions and explanations.
End with a clear '3 Key Takeaways to Remember' summary.
Connect theory directly to a DevSubnet tool so students can experiment.

topics.title: IP Address vs MAC Address: The Postal Mail Analogy Explained Simply
topics.analogy: Your MAC address is your Social Security Number (burned in permanently); your IP address is your current postal street address (changes when you move).

topics.title: What is a Default Gateway? The Exit Door of Your Local Network
topics.analogy: The exit turnstile of an office building: if a letter is for someone inside the room you hand it directly; if it's for anyone outside, you must hand it to the turnstile guard.

topics.title: How DNS Works: The Internet's Giant Contact List
topics.analogy: A phonebook or smartphone contacts list: humans remember names like 'google.com', but routers only dial numbers like '142.250.190.46'.

topics.title: TCP vs UDP: The Certified Letter vs the Postcard
topics.analogy: TCP is certified mail requiring a physical signature and re-sending if lost; UDP is a live sports broadcast or radio postcard where speed matters more than catching every frame.

topics.title: What Are Port Numbers? The Hotel Room Analogy
topics.analogy: The IP address is the hotel's street address; the Port number is the specific room number inside the hotel.

topics.title: Why Does IPv6 Have Letters? Hexadecimal Numbers Made Simple
topics.analogy: Counting on 10 fingers vs using a 16-color crayon box. Why computer scientists use A-F as shorthand for 4 binary bits.

topics.title: Subnetting Explained Like Slicing a Pizza
topics.analogy: Cutting a large whole pizza in half, then quarters, then eighths: each cut doubles the number of slices while halving the size of each slice.

topics.title: What is a Broadcast Storm? The Megaphone Echo Chamber
topics.analogy: What happens if someone shouts through a megaphone in a crowded stadium and 10 other people immediately repeat it into their own megaphones.

topics.title: The Story of the 'Ping': How Mike Muuss Named It After Sonar
topics.analogy: Submarine sonar sending out an acoustic sound pulse and listening for the underwater echo ping.

topics.title: From ALOHAnet to Ethernet: The Hawaiian Origins of Wi-Fi and LANs
topics.analogy: How researchers in Hawaii connecting islands via radio transmitters solved the problem of two people trying to talk at the exact same moment.
